problems.title: The stars observed with the telescope

figures.alt: Drawing of a refracting telescope: three parallel rays labelled "Incident light" enter a large converging lens labelled "Objective lens", converge to a focus and pass through a small lens labelled "Ocular lens" into a drawn human eye.

solution.statement:
The degree of collection of light from a star, $g_c$, by a telescop, used as shown in the drawing in Figure 1, is defined as the ratio of the area of the circle's surface, whose diameter is equal to the diameter of the lens of the telescope, and the area of the circle, whose diameter is equal to the diameter of the pupil of the observer's eye:

![](p1-sol-fig1)

$$g_c=\frac{\frac\pi4D_{\text{objectiv telescope}}^2}{\frac\pi4D_{\text{pupil eye}}^2}=\left(\frac{D_{\text{objectiv telescope}}}{D_{\text{pupil eye}}}\right)^2;\qquad D_{\text{objectiv telescope}}>D_{\text{pupil eye}};\quad g_c>1.$$

figures.alt: Objective and ocular lens ray diagram with observer eye.
figures.caption: Fig. 1

problems.title: The Sun on the Horizon
problems.statement:
The astronomical refraction correction, $\rho_{\mathrm{r}}$, has the minimum value, $\rho_{\mathrm{r,min}} = 0$, when the star is at the zenith of the Earth's surface observer $\left(z = 0; h = 90^{0}\right)$, and has the maximum value, $\rho_{\mathrm{r,max}}$, when the star, whose light passes through the Earth's atmosphere, in order to reach the Earth's surface observer, is at the horizon $\left(z = 90^{0}; h = 0\right)$, that is, when the star rises or sets.

It is known, that for an observer, atmospheric refraction raises the Sun in the moments of sunrise and sunset, that is, when it is below the horizon, approximately at its edge, by an apparent disk.

It is given: the radius of the Sun, $R_S = 6.96 \cdot 10^{5}\ km$ the distance between the centre of the Earth and the centre of the Sun, $d = 15 \cdot 10^{7}\ km$.

The value of $\rho_{r,max}$ ,is:

a) $\rho_{r,max} \approx 23.7'$

b) $\rho_{r,max} \approx 43.7'$

c) $\rho_{r,max} \approx 53.7'$

d) $\rho_{r,max} \approx 33.7'$

solution.statement:
Atmospheric refraction raises the Sun above its horizon, at its limit, at sunrise and sunset, approximately, with an apparent disk, as shown in the drawing in Figure 1.

![](p2-sol-fig1)

Therefore, in reality, the rising of the upper arc of the Sun's disk begins after the moment when we already see the entire solar disk above the horizon. We see the sunrise and sunset, later than they actually occur, which makes the day a little longer.

I mean, I see the disk of the whole Sun above the horizon, at its limit, but the Sun has not yet risen, it is still below the horizon !

I mean, the sun went down, it went down below the horizon, at the edge of it, but I still see the whole disk of it above the horizon !

Under these conditions, the astronomical refraction has the maximum value :

$$\rho_{\mathrm{r,max}}=\theta_S;$$

$$\sin\frac{\theta_S}2=\frac{R_S}d\approx\frac{\theta_S}2;$$

$$\theta_S=\frac{2R_S}d=\frac{2\cdot6.96\cdot10^5\ \mathrm{km}}{15\cdot10^7\ \mathrm{km}}=0.0098\ \text{radian};$$

$$1\ \mathrm{rad}=\frac{180\cdot60'}{3.14};$$

$$\theta_S=0.0098\cdot\frac{180\cdot60'}{3.14}\approx33.7'=\rho_{\mathrm{r,max}},$$

which proves that the value of the maximum astronomical refraction correction, $\rho_{\mathrm{r,max}}$, is approximately equal to the apparent angular diameter of the Sun, $\theta_S$.

figures.alt: Apparent and actual solar disks at the horizon with full explanatory labels.
figures.caption: Fig. 1

problems.title: The escape velocity
problems.statement:
*It is given:* $V_0 \approx 30\,\dfrac{\mathrm{km}}{\mathrm{s}}$, the speed of the Earth in its circular orbit around the Sun; $v_0 \approx 7.9\ \frac{\mathrm{km}}{s}$, the speed of a terrestrial satellite orbiting the Earth in a very low circular orbit (the first cosmic speed).

*It is known that*: $\dfrac{M_{\mathrm{Earth}}}{R_{\mathrm{Earth}}} \ll \dfrac{M_{\mathrm{Sun}}}{R_{\mathrm{Earth-Sun}}}$.

The variation of the kinetic energy of the body, in relation to the Sun, is neglected during the motion of the body from the surface of the Earth to the limit of the gravitational attraction of the Earth.
The approximate minimum escape velocity of a body B, relative to the Sun, launched at a distance from the Sun equal to *1 AU*, so that it leaves the Solar System forever, is:

a) $v_B \approx 45.52\ \frac{\mathrm{km}}{s}$

b) $v_B \approx 32.32\ \frac{\mathrm{km}}{s}$

c) $v_B \approx 22.22\ \frac{\mathrm{km}}{s}$

d) $v_B \approx 42.42\ \frac{\mathrm{km}}{s}$.

solution.statement:
Let $\vec v_B$ the speed of body B at the time of its launch from Earth, in relation to the Sun, so that the body reaches the limit of the gravitational attraction of the Sun and there it is at rest in relation to the Sun. Using the details in Figure 1, in accordance with the law of conservation of mechanical energy, it follows:

![](p3-sol-fig1)

$$R_E\ll R_{ES};$$

$$\frac{mv_B^2}2-K\frac{mM_E}{R_E}-K\frac{mM_S}{R_{ES}}=0;$$

$$\frac{M_E}{R_E}\ll\frac{M_S}{R_{ES}};$$

$$\frac{mv_B^2}2-K\frac{mM_S}{R_{ES}}=0;$$

$$v_B=\sqrt2\sqrt{K\frac{M_S}{R_{ES}}};$$

$$\sqrt{K\frac{M_S}{R_{ES}}}=v_{ES}=V_{\mathrm{orbital}}=V_0,$$

representing the orbital speed of the Earth on the circular trajectory around the Sun;

$$v_B=\sqrt2\,V_0,$$

representing the second cosmic speed in relation to the Sun (parabolic speed);

$$R_{ES}\approx1.5\cdot10^8\ \mathrm{km};\quad T_{ES}=1\ \text{year};$$

$$V_0=\frac{2\pi R_{ES}}{T_S}\approx30\ \mathrm{km/s};\qquad v_B\approx42.42\ \mathrm{km/s}.$$

*Conclusion:* the body launched from the Earth, reaches the limit of the gravitational attraction of the Sun, in relation to the Sun, on a parabolic trajectory, with the Sun in its focus.

figures.alt: Parabolic escape trajectory from Earth around the Sun.
figures.caption: Fig. 1

problems.title: The Terrestrial Satellite
problems.statement:
A small satellite (a luminous sphere) that orbits the Earth, in an equatorial circular orbit at the altitude $h$, is photographed with a camera on the ground, the lens of which is a converging lens with focal length $f$. The photography is made when the satellite aligns with the camera and the centre of the Earth.

*It is given:* the mass of the Earth, $M$; the gravitational constant, *G,* the radius of the Earth, *R*. During the photographic exposure the proper rotation of the Earth is neglected.

The length of the image on the photograph, after developing the photographic plate, placed in the focal plane of the objective lens, as indicated by the drawing in figure 1, if the exposure time of the camera was $\Delta t$, is given by the expression:

a) $l = \frac{f}{h-f} \cdot \sqrt{G\,\frac{M}{R+h}} \cdot \Delta t$

b) $l = \frac{f}{h+f} \cdot \sqrt{G\,\frac{M}{R+h}} \cdot \Delta t$

c) $l = \frac{f}{h-f} \cdot \sqrt{G\,\frac{M}{h-R}} \cdot \Delta t$

d) $l = \frac{f}{h-f} \cdot \sqrt{2G\,\frac{M}{R+h}} \cdot \Delta t$

figures.alt: Sketch of a camera: a double-headed arrow on the left labelled "Obiective lens", a rectangle labelled "Plate photografic", a grey bar on the right labelled "Focal plane of the objective lens", and a dashed brace above marked f for the focal length.
figures.caption: Fig. 1

solution.statement:
Sector AB, in the circular orbit of the satellite, represented in the drawing in Figure 2, traveled by the satellite during the time $\Delta t$, equal to the exposure time of the camera, has the length:

![](p4-sol-fig1)

$$\mathrm{AB}=v_{\mathrm{rel}}\cdot\Delta t,$$

where $v$ – the speed of the satellite in its circular orbit, relative to the center of the Earth;

$$K\frac{mM}{r^2}=\frac{mv^2}r;$$

$$v=\sqrt{K\frac Mr}=\sqrt{K\frac M{R+h}}.$$

Because the distance between the satellite and the camera lens is very large, the image will be formed in the focal plane of the camera lens.

Since the circle sector AB is very short and has a very large radius $(r=R+h)$, it can be assimilated with the line segment AB, so that:

$$\Delta(\mathrm{ACS})\sim\Delta(\mathrm{A'CS'});$$

$$\frac{\mathrm{A'S'}}{\mathrm{AS}}=\frac{\mathrm{CS'}}{\mathrm{CS}};\qquad\frac{l/2}{v\cdot\Delta t/2}=\frac f{h-f},$$

where $l$ – the length of the image on the photo;

$$l=\frac f{h-f}\cdot v\cdot\Delta t;$$

$$l=\frac f{h-f}\cdot\sqrt{K\frac M{R+h}}\cdot\Delta t.$$

figures.alt: Satellite arc and camera imaging geometry with all dimensions.
figures.caption: Fig. 1

problems.title: Andromeda Galaxy Rotation
problems.statement:
The following are known: the Earth – Andromeda galaxy distance, $R = 1.42 \cdot 10^{11} R_0$ , where $R_0$ is the radius of the Earth's circular orbit around the Sun; the mass of our Galaxy, $M_{\mathrm{G}} = 2.5 \cdot 10^{11} M_0$, where $M_0$ is the mass of the Sun; $T_0 =$ 1 terrestrial year, the period of rotation of the Earth around the Sun; the mass of the Andromeda galaxy, $M_{\mathrm{A}} = 3.6 \cdot 10^{11} M_0$.
The period of the rotational motions of our galaxy and the Andromeda galaxy, around their common centre of mass, is:

a) $5.1 \cdot 10^{10}$ years

b) $6.9 \cdot 10^{10}$ years

c) $7.9 \cdot 10^{10}$ years

d) $8.2 \cdot 10^{10}$ years

sections.title: Archived Grid 5 variant: Andromeda Constellation Rotation
sections.statement:
Our galaxy and the constellation Andromeda can be observed with the help of a telescope whose mirror has a diameter of $D=6\ \mathrm m$.

The following are known: the Earth - Andromeda distance, $R=1.42\cdot10^{11}R_0$, where $R_0$ is the radius of the Earth's circular orbit around the Sun; the mass of our Galaxy, $M_G=2.5\cdot10^{11}M_0$, where $M_0$ is the mass of the Sun; $T_0=1$ terrestrial year, the period of rotation of the Earth around the Sun; the mass of the constellation Andromeda, $M_A=3.6\cdot10^{11}M_0$.

*Knowing that:*

1) the photos were taken in visible light, with a wavelength $\lambda=5\cdot10^{-7}\ \mathrm m$;

2) the angular distance between two objects for which they can be observed separately is $\varphi_0=1.22\cdot\lambda/D$.

Using the photographs thus obtained, time required to highlight the rotational motions of our galaxy and the constellation Andromeda around their common center of mass, is:

a) $10^4$ ani; **b)** $10^3$ ani; c) $10^5$ ani; d) $10^4$ ani.

sections.title: Solution supplied for the archived Grid 5 variant
sections.statement:
From the study of light diffraction it is known that the angular distance between two objects for which they can be observed separately is approximately. $\lambda/D$. It means that the change in the position of the constellation Andromeda can be observed if its angular displacement is:

$$\varphi_0=1.22\cdot\frac\lambda D=1.22\cdot\frac{5\cdot10^{-7}}6=10.16\cdot10^{-8}\ \text{radians}.$$

If $T$ is the period of rotation of our Galaxy and the Andromeda Constellation, respectively, around their common center of mass, then the time required for the angular displacement $\varphi_0$ of the Andromeda constellation is:

$$\tau=\frac{\varphi_0}\omega=\frac{\varphi_0}{2\pi}T.$$

For two binary systems, using the generalized form of Kepler's third law, we can write that:

$$\left(\frac{T_1}{T_2}\right)^2\left(\frac{M_1+m_1}{M_2+m_2}\right)=\left(\frac{a_1}{a_2}\right)^3,$$

out of which, for the galaxy - Andromeda and Sun - Earth systems, results in:

$$\left(\frac T{T_0}\right)^2\left(\frac{M_G+M_A}{M_0+M_P}\right)=\left(\frac R{R_0}\right)^3;\quad M_P\ll M_0;\quad T_0=1\ \text{terrestrial year};$$

$$\left(\frac T{T_0}\right)^2\left(\frac{M_G+M_A}{M_0}\right)=\left(\frac R{R_0}\right)^3;$$

$$T^2=T_0^2\cdot\left(\frac R{R_0}\right)^3\cdot\left(\frac{M_0}{M_G+M_A}\right);\quad\tau=\frac{\varphi_0}{2\pi}T;\quad\varphi_0=1.22\cdot\frac\lambda D;$$

$$\tau=1.22\cdot\frac\lambda{2\pi D}T_0\left(\frac R{R_0}\right)^{3/2}\left(\frac{M_0}{M_G+M_A}\right)^{1/2}\approx10^3\ \text{years}.$$

solution.incompleteReason: The archived Grid_5.pdf solves the time to resolve angular motion with a 6 m telescope, not the rotation period requested here. Its complete variant and derivation are retained below; no official numerical answer for this final version was supplied.

problems.title: The Sun as seen from Saturn
problems.statement:
*It is known that*: the distance Saturn - Sun is 9.54 times greater than the distance Earth - Sun; the angular diameter of the Sun's disk, seen from Earth, is 32'.
The angular diameter of the Sun seen from Saturn, is:

a) $\alpha_{\mathrm{Sun-Saturn}} \approx 0.001$ radian

b) $\alpha_{\mathrm{Sun-Saturn}} \approx 0.002$ radian

c) $\alpha_{\mathrm{Sun-Saturn}} \approx 0.003$ radian

d) $\alpha_{\mathrm{Sun-Saturn}} \approx 0.004$ radian

solution.statement:
Since the distance between Saturn and the Sun is 9.54 times greater than the distance from Earth to the Sun, it turns out that the angular diameter of the Sun's disk, observed from Saturn, is 9.54 times smaller than the angular diameter of the Sun, observed from Earth. so that, using the drawing in Figure 1, it results:

![](p6-sol-fig1)

$$d_{\mathrm{Sun}}=r_{\mathrm{Saturn-Sun}}\alpha_{\mathrm{Sun-Saturn}};$$

$$d_{\mathrm{Sun}}=r_{\mathrm{Earth-Sun}}\alpha_{\mathrm{Sun-Earth}};$$

$$r_{\mathrm{Saturn-Sun}}=9.54r_{\mathrm{Earth-Sun}};$$

$$\alpha_{\mathrm{Sun-Saturn}}=\frac1{9.54}\alpha_{\mathrm{Sun-Earth}}=\frac{32'}{9.54}\approx3.35'\approx0.00097\ \text{radian};$$

$$\alpha_{\mathrm{Sun-Saturn}}\approx0.001\ \text{radian},$$

representing the angular diameter of the Sun seen from Saturn.

figures.alt: Comparison of the angular diameters of the Sun seen from Saturn and Earth.
figures.caption: Fig. 1

problems.title: Balls Suspended inside a Terrestrial Satellite
problems.statement:
An artificial satellite moves around the Earth in a circular orbit with radius *r.* We observe the satellite at the position and orientation shown in figure 1. Inside the satellite are suspended, by very light wires, four identical spherical balls, each with mass *m*, such that the balls (b) and (c) are symmetrical to the ball (a), the balls (a) and (d) are symmetrical to the ball (c), and the difference of their distances to the center of the Earth is $\Delta r = 2d$.

It is given: $M -$ the mass of the Earth; $G-$ gravitational attraction constant.

The tension in each suspension wire, is:

a) $T_{(\mathrm{a})} = 0; T_{(b)} = 3G\,\frac{mMd}{r^3} > 0; T_{(c)} = 3G\,\frac{mMd}{r^3} > 0;\ T_{(d)} = 0$

b) $T_{(a)} = G\,\frac{mMd}{r^3};\ T_{(b)} = G\,\frac{mMd}{r^3} > 0;\ T_{(c)} = G\,\frac{mMd}{r^3} > 0;\ T_{(d)} = G\,\frac{mMd}{r^3}$

c) $T_{(a)} = 3G\,\frac{mMd}{r^3} > 0;\ T_{(b)} = 0;\ T_{(c)} = 0;\ T_{(d)} = 3G\,\frac{mMd}{r^3} > 0$

d) $T_{(a)} = 2G\,\frac{mMd}{r^3} > 0; T_{(b)} = 2G\,\frac{mMd}{r^3} > 0;\ T_{(c)} = 2G\,\frac{mMd}{r^3} > 0;\ T_{(d)} = 2G\,\frac{mMd}{r^3} > 0$.

figures.alt: A cartoon rocket moving to the right (arrow) along a dashed semicircular orbit centred on the Earth, a black dot P; two further dashed semicircles lie inside and outside it, with radii marked r − d, r and r + d, and S at the lower right. Four balls a, b, c, d hang on wires inside the rocket, with dashed lines from each to the Earth's centre.
figures.caption: Fig. 1

solution.statement:
The orientation of the spacecraft being constant, and it is, as a whole, a rigid solid body, means that all points belonging to the spacecraft move around the Earth at the same angular velocity, $\omega$, whose expression is obtained as follows:

$$F_{\mathrm{ag(NC)}}=K\frac{m_{(NC)}M}{r^2}=m_{(NC)}\omega^2r;\qquad\omega^2=K\frac M{r^3}.$$

The centripetal accelerations of the three suspended balls are:

$$a_{\mathrm{cp(a)}}=\omega^2r;\quad a_{\mathrm{cp(b)}}=\omega^2(r-d);\quad a_{\mathrm{cp(c)}}=\omega^2(r+d);\quad a_{\mathrm{cp(d)}}=\omega^2r=a_{\mathrm{cp(a)}}.$$

Assuming that all the suspension wires are tensioned, then, for each ball, the resultant of the gravitational pull force with the tension in the respective suspension wire is the centripetal force responsible for the circular motion of each ball.

Results that:

sections.title: for the ball (a)
sections.statement:
$$\vec F_{\mathrm{cp(a)}}=\vec F_{\mathrm{ag(a)}}+\vec T_{(a)};\quad F_{\mathrm{cp(a)}}=F_{\mathrm{ag(a)}}-T_{(a)};\quad T_{(a)}=F_{\mathrm{ag(a)}}-F_{\mathrm{cp(a)}};$$

$$F_{\mathrm{ag(a)}}=K\frac{mM}{r^2};\quad F_{\mathrm{cp(a)}}=ma_{\mathrm{cp(a)}}=m\omega^2r;\quad\omega^2=K\frac M{r^3};\quad F_{\mathrm{cp(a)}}=ma_{\mathrm{cp(a)}}=K\frac{mM}{r^2};$$

$$T_{(a)}=K\frac{mM}{r^2}-K\frac{mM}{r^2};$$

$$T_{(a)}=0,$$

which means that the suspension wire of the ball (a) is not tensioned, so that the ball (a) is in a weightless state;

sections.title: for the ball (b)
sections.statement:
$$\vec F_{\mathrm{cp(b)}}=\vec F_{\mathrm{ag(b)}}+\vec T_{(b)};\quad F_{\mathrm{cp(b)}}=F_{\mathrm{ag(b)}}-T_{(b)};\quad T_{(b)}=F_{\mathrm{ag(b)}}-F_{\mathrm{cp(b)}};$$

$$F_{\mathrm{ag(b)}}=K\frac{mM}{(r-d)^2}=K\frac{mM}{r^2(1-d/r)^2}=K\frac M{r^2}\left(1-\frac dr\right)^{-2};$$

$$d\ll r;\qquad\left(1-\frac dr\right)^{-2}\approx1+2\cdot\frac dr;$$

$$F_{\mathrm{ag(b)}}=K\frac M{r^2}\left(1+2\cdot\frac dr\right);$$

$$F_{\mathrm{cp(b)}}=ma_{\mathrm{cp(b)}};\quad a_{\mathrm{cp(b)}}=\omega^2(r-d);\quad F_{\mathrm{cp(b)}}=m\omega^2(r-d);$$

$$\omega^2=K\frac M{r^3};\qquad F_{\mathrm{cp(b)}}=K\frac{mM}{r^3}(r-d);$$

$$\begin{aligned}T_{(b)}&=K\frac M{r^2}\left(1+2\cdot\frac dr\right)-K\frac{mM}{r^3}(r-d)\\&=K\frac{mM}{r^2}+2K\frac{mMd}{r^3}-K\frac{mM}{r^2}+K\frac{mMd}{r^3};\end{aligned}$$

$$T_{(b)}=3K\frac{mMd}{r^3}\ne0;\qquad T_{(b)}=3K\frac{mMd}{r^3}>0,$$

which means that the ball suspension wire (b) is tensioned so that the ball (b) is not weightless;

sections.title: for the ball (c)
sections.statement:
$$\vec F_{\mathrm{cp(c)}}=\vec F_{\mathrm{ag(c)}}+\vec T_{(c)};\quad F_{\mathrm{cp(c)}}=F_{\mathrm{ag(c)}}+T_{(c)};\quad T_{(c)}=F_{\mathrm{cp(c)}}-F_{\mathrm{ag(c)}};$$

$$F_{\mathrm{ag(c)}}=K\frac{mM}{(r+d)^2}=K\frac{mM}{r^2(1+d/r)^2}=K\frac{mM}{r^2}\left(1+\frac dr\right)^{-2};$$

$$d\ll r;\qquad\left(1+\frac dr\right)^{-2}\approx1-2\cdot\frac dr;$$

$$F_{\mathrm{ag(c)}}=K\frac{mM}{r^2}\left(1-2\cdot\frac dr\right);$$

$$F_{\mathrm{cp(c)}}=ma_{\mathrm{cp(c)}};\quad a_{\mathrm{cp(c)}}=\omega^2(r+d);\quad F_{\mathrm{cp(c)}}=m\omega^2(r+d);$$

$$\omega^2=K\frac M{r^3};\qquad F_{\mathrm{cp(c)}}=K\frac{mM}{r^3}(r+d);$$

$$\begin{aligned}T_{(c)}&=K\frac{mM}{r^3}(r+d)-K\frac{mM}{r^2}\left(1-2\cdot\frac dr\right)\\&=K\frac{mM}{r^2}+K\frac{mMd}{r^3}-K\frac{mM}{r^2}+2K\frac{mMd}{r^3};\end{aligned}$$

$$T_{(c)}=-3K\frac{mMd}{r^3}\ne0;\qquad T_{(c)}=3K\frac{mMd}{r^3}>0,$$

which means that the ball suspension wire (c) is tensioned so that the ball (c) is not weightless;

sections.title: for the ball (d)
sections.statement:
$$\vec F_{\mathrm{cp(d)}}=\vec F_{\mathrm{ag(d)}}+\vec T_{(d)};\quad F_{\mathrm{cp(d)}}=F_{\mathrm{ag(d)}}+T_{(d)};\quad T_{(d)}=F_{\mathrm{cp(d)}}-F_{\mathrm{ag(d)}};$$

$$F_{\mathrm{ag(d)}}=K\frac{mM}{r^2};\quad F_{\mathrm{cp(d)}}=ma_{\mathrm{cp(d)}}=m\omega^2r;\quad\omega^2=K\frac M{r^3};\quad F_{\mathrm{cp(d)}}=ma_{\mathrm{cp(d)}}=K\frac{mM}{r^2};$$

$$T_{(d)}=K\frac{mM}{r^2}-K\frac{mM}{r^2};$$

$$T_{(d)}=0,$$

which means that the suspension wire of the ball (d) is not tensioned, so that the ball (d) is in a weightless state.

problems.title: Spaceship to the Sun
problems.statement:
In a future program, NASA plans to launch a spacecraft, aimed directly at the Sun, without a human crew, to gather information, on its way to the Sun, both about all the inner planets and, in particular, about the Sun.
They are known: the distance Earth - Sun, $r_{\mathrm{ES}} = 1.5 \cdot 10^{11}\ \mathrm{m}$; the period of the Earth's rotation around the Sun, $T_{\mathrm{E}} = 3.15 \cdot 10^{7}\ \mathrm{s}$; the radius of the Sun, $R_{\mathrm{S}} \approx \dfrac{r_{\mathrm{ES}}}{200}$.
If the launch of the spacecraft will be done in such a way that its motion relative to the Sun is a free fall, then the approximate duration of the Earth-Sun flight is:

a) $t \approx 3.6 \cdot 10^{5}\ s$

b) $t \approx 6.6 \cdot 10^{6}\ s$

c) $t \approx 5.6 \cdot 10^{6}\ s$

d) $t \approx 4.6 \cdot 10^{6}\ s$

solution.statement:
Imagine that a spacecraft is launched from the Earth whose speed in relation to the Sun is slightly lower than the orbital speed of the Earth in relation to the Sun. The ship will evolve around the Sun in an elliptical trajectory, with the Sun in the focus opposite the launch point. The lower this initial speed of the ship, the longer the ellipse on which the spacecraft will evolve around the Sun will be longer. For a certain value of this speed, the spacecraft, in its elliptical motion around the Sun, will touch the surface of the Sun, as shown in Figure 1. In this case, the height of the ship's orbit is equal to the Sun's radius. which we know is:

$$r_{\min}=R_S\approx\frac{r_{ES}}{200}.$$

As a result, the semi-axes of the ship's elliptical orbit, tangent to the Sun's surface, are a and b $\ll$ a, respectively, so that the small half-axis of this elliptical orbit can be neglected $(b\approx0)$. Under these conditions, the trajectory of the ship in relation to the Sun can be estimated to be rectilinear, joining the launching point of the ship with the Sun, so that the ship will reach the surface of the Sun, in point B, after a free fall towards it.

*Conclusion:* In order for the ship to fall freely on the surface of the Sun, in point B, after a rectilinear course in relation to it, at the initial moment of its launch from the surface of the Earth, the speed of the ship in relation to the Sun must have been zero.

To meet this condition, it is necessary that at the time of launching the ship from the Earth's surface, a speed relative to the Earth be imprinted on the ship, so that the speed of the ship relative to the Sun is zero.

The Earth's launch velocity relative to Earth must be inversely related to the orientation of the Earth's orbital velocity relative to the Sun, as shown in Figure b in Figure 1, and their modulus must be equal:

$$v_{ES}=\frac{2\pi r_{ES}}{T_E}=\frac{2\cdot3.14\cdot1.5\cdot10^{11}\ \mathrm m}{3.15\cdot10^7\ \mathrm s}\approx3\cdot10^4\ \mathrm{m/s}=30\ \mathrm{km/s}.$$

![](p8-sol-fig1)

According to Kepler's third law, it can be written that:

$$\frac{T_E^2}{r_{ES}^3}=\frac{T_{NC}^2}{(r_{ES}/2)^3},$$

where $T_{NC}$ is the period of the spacecraft's motion on the elongated elliptical trajectory around the Sun;

$$T_{NC}=\frac{T_E}{2\sqrt2},$$

so that the duration of the free fall of the ship on the surface of the Sun is:

$$t=\frac{T_{NC}}2=\frac{T_E}{4\sqrt2}\approx5.6\cdot10^6\ \mathrm s.$$

figures.alt: Elliptical and limiting radial spacecraft trajectories toward the Sun.
figures.caption: Fig. 1

problems.title: The Moon, seen on the way to the Moon
problems.statement:
The full Moon, whose linear diameter is $d = 3\,436\ \mathrm{km}$, at Earth in the distance $r_0 = 384\,000\ km$, has the apparent magnitude $m_0 = -12.7$. The apparent magnitude of the Sun, seen from Earth, is $m_{\mathrm{s}} = -26.84$.
The distance, *r*, from the full Moon, where a cosmonaut is, on the way of his spaceship to the Moon, the magnitude of the full Moon should be 50% of the magnitude of the Sun as seen from Earth, is:

a) $r \approx 198\,243\ km\ ss$

b) $r \approx 320\,732\ km$

c) $r \approx 132\,521\ km$

d) $r \approx 275\,633\ km$

sections.title: Archived Grid 9 variant: equal brightness
sections.statement:
The Moon, whose linear diameter is $d=3436\ \mathrm{km}$, at Earth in the distance $r_0=348000\ \mathrm{km}$, has the apparent magnitude $m_0=-12.7$. The apparent magnitude of the Sun, seen from Earth, is $m_s=-26.84$.

The distance, $r$, from the Moon, where a cosmonaut is, on the way of his spaceship to the Moon, the brightness of the Moon should be the same as the brightness of the Sun seen from Earth, is:

a) $r\approx675.25\ \mathrm{km}$; **b)** $r\approx568.88\ \mathrm{km}$; c) $r\approx763.23\ \mathrm{km}$; d) $r\approx837.44\ \mathrm{km}$.

sections.title: Solution supplied for the archived Grid 9 variant
sections.statement:
The approach of the cosmonaut to the Moon must be such that it determines a variation of the apparent magnitude of the Moon:

$$\Delta m=m-m_0=m_S-m_0=-26.84-(-12.7)=-14.14,$$

so that the apparent magnitude of the Moon, viewed from this new distance, is:

$$m=m_0+\Delta m=m_S=-26.84;$$

$$\Delta m=m_S-m_0=-26.84+12.7=-14.14.$$

Knowing that the luminous intensity, $I$, of a star, in particular of the Moon, is:

$$I=\frac\phi\Omega=\frac L\Omega=\frac W{t\cdot\Omega},$$

that is, the energy flow emitted by the star, the Moon, in the unit of solid angle, then:

$$\Omega=\frac A{\Delta^2};\quad A=\Omega\cdot\Delta^2;\quad\phi=I\cdot\Omega;\quad E=\frac\phi A=\frac{I\cdot\Omega}{\Omega\cdot\Delta^2}=\frac I{\Delta^2};\quad E=\frac L{4\pi\Delta^2}.$$

According to Pogson's formula, if $E_0$ and respectively $E$ are the brightnesses of the Moon, corresponding to the initial $(r_0)$ and respectively the final distances $(r)$, shown in the drawing in figure 1, it results:

![](p9-sol-fig1)

$$\log\frac E{E_0}=-0.4\cdot(m-m_0)=\log10^{-0.4(m-m_0)};\quad E_0=\frac I{r_0^2};\quad E=\frac I{r^2},$$

where $I$ is the luminous intensity of the Moon;

$$\log\frac{r_0^2}{r^2}=\log10^{-0.4(m-m_0)};$$

$$2\log\frac{r_0}r=-0.4\cdot\Delta m;\qquad\log\frac{r_0}r=0.2\cdot14.14=2.828=\log10^{2.828};$$

$$\frac{r_0}r=10^{2.828};\qquad r=\frac{r_0}{10^{2.828}};$$

$$x=10^{2.828};\quad\log x=2.828;\quad x\approx675;$$

$$r=\frac{r_0}{10^{2.828}};\qquad10^{2.828}\approx675;$$

$$r=\frac{r_0}{675}=\frac{384000\ \mathrm{km}}{675}\approx568.88\ \mathrm{km},$$

this is the distance from which the Moon should be viewed, so that its brightness is the same as the brightness of the Sun, seen from Earth.

problems.title: The luminosity of a star

solution.statement:
The luminosity of a star, meaning the energy of the total radiation emitted by that star, in the unit of time, through its entire surface, at all wavelengths, in accordance with the Stefan-Boltzmann law, results:

$$L_\Sigma=100\cdot L_S;$$

$$L_\Sigma=4\pi\cdot R_\Sigma^2\cdot\sigma\cdot T_\Sigma^4;\qquad L_S=4\pi\cdot R_S^2\cdot\sigma\cdot T_S^4;$$

$$4\pi\cdot R_\Sigma^2\cdot\sigma\cdot T_\Sigma^4=10^2\cdot4\pi\cdot R_S^2\cdot\sigma\cdot T_S^4;\qquad R_\Sigma^2\cdot T_\Sigma^4=10^2\cdot R_S^2\cdot T_S^4;$$

$$\frac{R_\Sigma^2}{R_S^2}=10^2\cdot\frac{T_S^4}{T_\Sigma^4}=10^2\cdot\left(\frac{T_S}{T_\Sigma}\right)^4=10^2\cdot2^4;$$

$$\frac{R_\Sigma}{R_S}=40.$$
